argument_macro_structure.dominant_argument_form: Internal critique of a proposed Kantian justification for rebellion, using Kant's own principles to show that rebellion is categorically impermissible.
argument_macro_structure.premise_explicitness: High: premises are explicitly stated and defended through textual interpretation and logical analysis.

argumentative_quality.dialectical_reasonableness: High: engages with potential objections (good will, happiness, revised maxim) and resolves them within Kantian framework.
argumentative_quality.logical_relevance: High: all arguments directly support the thesis that Kantian ethics cannot justify rebellion.
argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: Moderate: depends on acceptance of Kantian moral theory and Korsgaard's interpretation; internal consistency is strong.

explicit_definitions_given: FUL: Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.
FKE: Act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in another, always as an end and never merely as a means.
Strict/perfect duty: negative, absolute, admits no exception.
Broad/imperfect duty: positive, requires adopting an end, allows latitude in means.

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Explicitly addresses objections: revised maxim, good will, happiness-based motivation, and Kant's enthusiasm for revolution.
objections_raised: Rebel might claim a good will justifies rebellion.
Rebel might appeal to happiness or improved justice as a consequence.
Kant's enthusiasm for the French Revolution seems to contradict his prohibition.
A revised maxim limited to egregious atrocities might pass universalization.

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: Textual interpretation, conceptual analysis, logical deduction from Kantian principles.
named_thought_experiments: Analogy of curing disease by poisoning the patient

philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Political obligation, moral permissibility of revolution, categorical imperative, kingdom of ends

structural_organization.structure_type: Problem-solution with progressive argumentation: introduction of paradox, exposition of Kantian framework, application to rebellion, refutation of objections, resolution of paradox, conclusion.

summary_of_core_decisions: The text argues that Kantian ethics cannot justify political rebellion because the rebel's maxim fails the universalization test, violates strict duties, treats the sovereign as a mere means, and cannot be an act of good will. Kant's enthusiasm for the French Revolution is reinterpreted as admiration for the spectators' moral disposition, not for the revolutionaries' action.

thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: Low: final paragraph is definitive and unqualified.
